decks.title: Straight Lines — Part 1: Slope, angle between lines and the first forms of an equation
goals: Find the slope of a line from its inclination or from two points
Use slopes to test parallel, perpendicular and collinear
Find the angle between two lines with the tangent formula
Write the equation of a line in point-slope and slope-intercept form
Find parallel and perpendicular lines through a point

slides.heading: Straight lines, Part 1: Direction and slope
slides.body_md: Every line through a point has a direction. How can a single number fix that direction, and how do we use it to write an equation?

visual.alt: Four lines through the point M (2, −1): y = x − 3 rises with slope 1; y = −2x + 3 falls with slope −2; y = −1 is horizontal with slope 0; and the dashed vertical line x = 2 has no slope.
visual.caption: One point, many directions: the slope fixes the direction.

slides.narration: Welcome. Look at four lines through the same point. One rises, one falls, one is flat and one stands straight up. What separates them is direction, and direction is measured by a number called the slope. In this part we use slope to test parallel and perpendicular lines, to find the angle between lines, and to write the first forms of an equation.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **slope** from an angle or from two points
Build lines **parallel** or **perpendicular** to a given line
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will find the slope of a line from its inclination or from two points on it. You will use slopes to test whether lines are parallel, perpendicular, or whether points lie on one line. You will find the angle between two lines, and you will write equations in point-slope and slope-intercept form.

slides.heading: Slope and inclination
slides.body_md: The **inclination** $\theta$ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis, measured anticlockwise, $0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$. Its **slope** is $m = \tan\theta$. A vertical line has no slope.

visual.alt: Table of inclinations and slopes: 0 degrees gives slope 0; 30 degrees gives one over root three; 45 degrees gives 1; 60 degrees gives root three; a vertical line at 90 degrees has no slope; 120 degrees gives minus root three; 135 degrees gives minus 1.
visual.caption: The slope is the tangent of the inclination.

slides.narration: The inclination of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x axis, measured anticlockwise. The slope is the tangent of that angle. A flat line has slope zero. At forty-five degrees the slope is one. Beyond ninety degrees the tangent is negative, so a falling line has a negative slope. A vertical line has no slope at all, because the tangent of ninety degrees is not defined.

slides.heading: Slope from two points
slides.body_md: For $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, the rise over the run. The order of the points does not matter.

visual.alt: The line through A (−3, −1) and B (5, 5) with a right-angled step under it: a horizontal run of 8 units from A, then a vertical rise of 6 units up to B. The slope is rise over run, six eighths, which is three quarters.
visual.caption: Slope $=$ rise $\div$ run $= \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

slides.narration: To find the slope from two points, subtract the coordinates in the same order and divide the change in y, the rise, by the change in x, the run. In the figure the run is eight and the rise is six, so the slope is three quarters. If you swap the two points, both differences change sign and the answer stays the same.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: slope and inclination
slides.body_md: Find the slope of the line through $P(-6, 1)$ and $Q(3, -5)$ and the angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis.

visual.alt: Worked example 1: the line through P (−6, 1) and Q (3, −5) falls from left to right. Its slope is minus two thirds, so its inclination is an obtuse angle of about 146.31 degrees.
visual.caption: A negative slope: the line falls, and the inclination is obtuse.

slides.narration: The rise from the first point to the second is minus six and the run is nine, so the slope is minus two thirds. A negative slope means the line falls from left to right, and the inclination is an obtuse angle. The tangent inverse of two thirds is about thirty-three point six nine degrees, so the inclination is that taken from one hundred eighty, about one hundred forty-six point three one degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a slope
slides.body_md: What is the slope of the line joining the points with coordinates minus five, four and three, minus eight?
slides.narration: Subtract in the same order and divide rise by run.

slides.heading: Parallel and perpendicular lines
slides.body_md: Two non-vertical lines with slopes $m_1$, $m_2$ are **parallel** if $m_1 = m_2$ and **perpendicular** if $m_1m_2 = -1$. A vertical line is perpendicular to a horizontal line.

visual.alt: Three lines: y = x/2 + 1 and y = x/2 − 2 are parallel, both with slope one half, and never meet; y = −2x + 6 has slope −2 and cuts the first line at M (2, 2) at right angles, because one half times minus two is minus one.
visual.caption: Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$. Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

slides.narration: Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is minus one, which means one slope is the negative reciprocal of the other. In the figure, the first two lines both have slope one half and never meet. The third has slope minus two, and one half times minus two is minus one, so it crosses the first line at right angles.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding k
slides.body_md: The line through $(k, -2)$ and $(4, 6)$ is compared with the line through $(-3, 1)$ and $(5, 5)$. Find $k$ if the lines are (i) parallel, (ii) perpendicular.

visual.alt: Table: intercepts 5 and minus 3 give x over 5 plus y over minus 3 equals 1; multiplying by 15 gives 3x minus 5y minus 15 equals 0, and the point minus 5, minus 6 satisfies it.
visual.caption: Intercepts are signed lengths along the axes.

slides.narration: The given line has slope one half. The other line has slope eight divided by four minus k. For parallel lines, set that equal to one half. Then four minus k is sixteen, and k is minus twelve. For perpendicular lines, set it equal to minus two, the negative reciprocal. Then four minus k is minus four, and k is eight.

slides.heading: Quick check: perpendicular lines
slides.body_md: True or false: the line through the origin and the point seven, minus four is perpendicular to the line through one, three and minus three, minus four.
slides.narration: Find both slopes and multiply them.

slides.heading: Angle between two lines
slides.body_md: If $\theta$ is the acute angle between lines of slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$, then $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$. If $1 + m_1m_2 = 0$ the lines are perpendicular. The obtuse angle is $180^\circ - \theta$.

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of slopes with the tangent of the acute angle between the lines: 2 and one third give tangent 1, 45 degrees; 1 and one third give one half, 26.57 degrees; 3 and minus one half give 7, 81.87 degrees; 2 and minus one half make 1 plus m one m two equal to zero, so the lines are perpendicular at 90 degrees.
visual.caption: $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$; if $1 + m_1m_2 = 0$ the lines are perpendicular.

slides.narration: The tangent of the acute angle between two lines is the size of the difference of the slopes, divided by one plus their product. The table tries four pairs of slopes. When the denominator is zero the lines are perpendicular. For the first pair the tangent is one and the angle is forty-five degrees. The other angle between the same two lines is its supplement.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the angle and the meeting point
slides.body_md: Find the acute angle between $x - 2y + 3 = 0$ and $2x - y - 3 = 0$, and the point where they meet.

visual.alt: Worked example 3: the lines x − 2y + 3 = 0 (slope one half) and 2x − y − 3 = 0 (slope 2) cross at P (3, 3). The tangent of the acute angle between them is three quarters, an angle of about 36.87 degrees.
visual.caption: Slopes $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $2$: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$, $\theta \approx 36.87^\circ$.

slides.narration: Solve each equation for y to read the slopes: one half and two. The tangent of the acute angle is the size of one half minus two, which is three halves, divided by one plus one, which is two. That gives three quarters, and an angle of about thirty-six point eight seven degrees. Solving the two equations together shows that the lines cross at the point three, three.

slides.heading: Quick check: an angle
slides.body_md: Two lines have slopes one half and one third. The tangent of the acute angle between them is ____.
slides.narration: Use the tangent formula.

slides.heading: Collinear points
slides.body_md: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ are **collinear** if the slope of $AB$ equals the slope of $BC$, since the two segments share $B$.

visual.alt: Three points D (−5, 4), E (1, 1) and F (7, −2) on one straight line. The slope of DE and the slope of EF are both minus one half, and they share the point E.
visual.caption: Equal slopes $DE$ and $EF$ with $E$ shared: collinear.

slides.narration: Three points lie on one straight line when the slope from the first to the second equals the slope from the second to the third. The figure shows three points whose two slopes are both minus one half. Because the second point is common to both segments, equal slopes force all three points onto a single line.

slides.heading: Point-slope form and special lines
slides.body_md: The line through $(x_1, y_1)$ with slope $m$ is $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$. A horizontal line is $y = k$; a vertical line is $x = h$.

visual.alt: The line through T (2, −3) with slope two thirds, so that a step of 3 units across is a rise of 2 units; it also passes through U (5, −1). Its equation is 2x − 3y − 13 = 0.
visual.caption: Point-slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.

slides.narration: If you know one point on a line and its slope, the equation is y minus y one equals m times x minus x one. The figure shows the line through the point two, minus three with slope two thirds. Horizontal lines have equations of the form y equals a constant, and vertical lines have equations of the form x equals a constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a parallel line
slides.body_md: Find the line through $(4, 1)$ that is parallel to the line through $(-1, -3)$ and $(2, 5)$.

rows: Parallel line has the same slope

visual.alt: Table: the line through minus 1, minus 3 and 2, 5 has slope eight thirds; the parallel line through 4, 1 is y minus 1 equals eight thirds times x minus 4, which is 8x minus 3y minus 29 equals 0.
visual.caption: A parallel line keeps the slope; only the point changes.

slides.narration: First find the slope of the given line: eight over three. A parallel line has the same slope. Now use the point-slope form through four, one. Multiply both sides by three to clear the fraction, and collect the terms to get eight x minus three y minus twenty-nine equals zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: a vertical line
slides.body_md: The line drawn through the point minus seven, two at right angles to the x-axis has which equation?
slides.narration: Think about which coordinate stays fixed.

slides.heading: Slope-intercept form
slides.body_md: A line with slope $m$ that meets the $y$-axis at $(0, c)$ has equation $y = mx + c$. The number $c$ is the **$y$-intercept**.

visual.alt: The line y = three quarters x − 2. It crosses the y-axis at C (0, −2), so the y-intercept is −2, and it passes through D (4, 1) and E (−4, −5): every 4 units across is a rise of 3 units.
visual.caption: In $y = mx + c$: slope $m = \dfrac{3}{4}$, $y$-intercept $c = -2$.

slides.narration: When the line meets the y axis at the point zero, c, the equation takes the neat form y equals m x plus c. The figure shows slope three quarters and y intercept minus two. Starting at the intercept, every four units to the right the line rises three units, which gives the other marked points.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a perpendicular line
slides.body_md: Find the line through $(3, -1)$ perpendicular to $2x + 5y - 4 = 0$.

visual.alt: Table: the line 2x plus 5y minus 4 equals 0 has slope minus two fifths, so a perpendicular has slope five halves; through 3, minus 1 it is y plus 1 equals five halves times x minus 3, which is 5x minus 2y minus 17 equals 0.
visual.caption: Perpendicular slope: the negative reciprocal.

slides.narration: Rewrite the given line as y equals minus two fifths x plus four fifths, so its slope is minus two fifths. The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, five halves. Use point-slope form through three, minus one, clear the fraction, and the equation is five x minus two y minus seventeen equals zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: collinear points
slides.body_md: True or false: the points minus two, minus seven; one, minus one; and four, five all lie on one straight line.
slides.narration: Compare the slopes of the two segments.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Slope $m = \tan\theta = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$; a vertical line has no slope
$\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$ for the acute angle
Collinear points have equal slopes between them
$y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ and $y = mx + c$

nodes.label: Forms: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, $y = mx + c$

visual.alt: Summary flow: the slope is the tangent of the inclination, found from two points; parallel lines have equal slopes and perpendicular lines have slope product minus one; the angle between lines uses the tangent formula; and the point-slope and slope-intercept forms write the equation.
visual.caption: Slope, angle and the first forms of the equation.

slides.narration: To sum up. The slope is the tangent of the inclination, found by rise over run. Parallel lines have equal slopes and perpendicular lines have slopes with product minus one. The tangent formula gives the acute angle between two lines. Collinear points have equal slopes between them. And the point-slope and slope-intercept forms give the equation of a line.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Slope or parallel test (1–2 marks):** show the subtraction and the value
**Angle between lines (2–3 marks):** slopes, the formula, then the angle
**Equation of a line (2–3 marks):** the form, the substitution, the simplified result
**Mistake:** forgetting the modulus in the angle formula
**Mistake:** using the negative of the slope instead of the negative reciprocal
slides.narration: In questions on slope, marks go for the formula, the substitution and the final value. For the angle between lines, write both slopes first. Three common slips: dividing run by rise, leaving out the absolute value in the tangent formula, and using the negative of the slope rather than the negative reciprocal for a perpendicular.

decks.title: Straight Lines — Part 2: More forms, distances and the normal form
goals: Write the two-point and intercept forms of an equation
Convert the general equation to other forms and read slope and intercepts
Find the distance of a point from a line
Find the distance between parallel lines
Reduce a line to normal form (formative only)

slides.heading: Straight lines, Part 2: Forms and distances
slides.body_md: A pipe must run from a well to a straight canal by the shortest route. How do we find that distance from the equation of the canal?

visual.alt: The line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 meets the axes at A (4, 0) and B (0, 3). The point Q (4, 5) is joined to the line by a perpendicular that meets it at F (1.6, 1.8); the length QF is 4 units, which is |12 + 20 − 12| over 5.
visual.caption: The distance is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the line.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here a point sits away from a line, and a perpendicular joins them. That perpendicular is the shortest route, and its length is the distance from the point to the line. We will first finish the forms of an equation, then find this distance, the distance between parallel lines, and meet the normal form.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Read slope and intercepts from the **general equation**
Find the **distance of a point** from a line
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will write the equation of a line through two points and from its intercepts. You will convert the general equation to other forms. You will find the distance of a point from a line and between two parallel lines. Finally you will meet the normal form, which is for practice and is not examined in the board paper.

slides.heading: Two-point form
slides.body_md: The line through $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ is $y - y_1 = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1)$. It is the point-slope form with the slope found from the two points.

visual.alt: The line through A (−3, −4) and B (6, 2). Its slope is six ninths, which is two thirds, and its equation is 2x − 3y − 6 = 0.
visual.caption: Two-point form: $y - y_1 = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1)$.

slides.narration: Given two points, first find the slope, then use the point-slope form with either point. The result is called the two-point form. The figure shows the line through minus three, minus four and six, two. It does not matter which point you use, and it is wise to check the other point in your answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two points
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through $A(-3, -4)$ and $B(6, 2)$.

visual.alt: Table: the line through minus 3, minus 4 and 6, 2 has slope two thirds; the two-point form gives 3y plus 12 equals 2x plus 6, so 2x minus 3y minus 6 equals 0, and the point 6, 2 satisfies it.
visual.caption: Always check the second point in the final equation.

slides.narration: The slope is six over nine, which is two thirds. Use the point minus three, minus four: y plus four equals two thirds of x plus three. Multiply by three and rearrange to get two x minus three y minus six equals zero. Check with the other point: two times six minus three times two minus six is zero, as it should be.

slides.heading: Quick check: the y-intercept
slides.body_md: The line through two, one and six, nine cuts the y axis at the point zero, ____.
slides.narration: Find the equation first, then put x equal to zero.

slides.heading: Intercept form
slides.body_md: A line with $x$-intercept $a$ and $y$-intercept $b$ (both nonzero) is $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$. Intercepts are signed: they can be negative.

visual.alt: The line with x-intercept 5 and y-intercept −3, through A (5, 0) and B (0, −3), and also through C (−5, −6). Its equation is x over 5 plus y over −3 equals 1, that is 3x − 5y − 15 = 0.
visual.caption: Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$.

slides.narration: If a line cuts the x axis at a and the y axis at b, its equation is x over a plus y over b equals one. In the figure a is five and b is minus three. Intercepts are signed lengths, so a line that cuts below the origin has a negative y intercept. A line through the origin has no intercept form.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from the intercepts
slides.body_md: Find the line with intercepts $5$ on the $x$-axis and $-3$ on the $y$-axis.

visual.alt: Table: intercepts 5 and minus 3 give x over 5 plus y over minus 3 equals 1; multiplying by 15 gives 3x minus 5y minus 15 equals 0, and the point minus 5, minus 6 satisfies it.
visual.caption: Intercepts are signed lengths along the axes.

slides.narration: Put a equal to five and b equal to minus three. The equation is x over five plus y over minus three equals one. Multiply every term by fifteen to clear the fractions, giving three x minus five y equals fifteen. As a check, the point minus five, minus six also satisfies the equation.

slides.heading: Quick check: from intercepts
slides.body_md: A straight line makes an intercept of minus four on the x axis and six on the y axis. Which equation is it?
slides.narration: Write the intercept form, then clear the fractions.

slides.heading: The general equation (formative)
slides.body_md: Every straight line has an equation $Ax + By + C = 0$ with $A$, $B$ not both zero. This slide is formative only: the slope is $-\dfrac{A}{B}$ and the intercepts are $-\dfrac{C}{A}$ and $-\dfrac{C}{B}$.

visual.alt: Table of the general equation A x plus B y plus C equals 0: the slope is minus A over B, the x-intercept is minus C over A and the y-intercept is minus C over B; if B is 0 the line is vertical, if A is 0 it is horizontal, and if C is 0 it passes through the origin.
visual.caption: One equation $Ax + By + C = 0$ covers every straight line.

slides.narration: Every straight line can be written as A x plus B y plus C equals zero. This idea is for practice and is not examined in the board paper, but it is useful. The slope is minus A over B. The intercepts are minus C over A on the x axis and minus C over B on the y axis. If B is zero the line is vertical, and if C is zero it passes through the origin.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: changing the form
slides.body_md: Reduce $3x - 4y + 24 = 0$ to slope-intercept and intercept forms.

visual.alt: Table for 3x minus 4y plus 24 equals 0: the slope-intercept form is y equals three quarters x plus 6; the intercept form is x over minus 8 plus y over 6 equals 1; the intercepts are minus 8 and 6.
visual.caption: Solve for $y$ for the slope; divide by $-C$ for the intercepts.

slides.narration: To get the slope-intercept form, solve for y: four y equals three x plus twenty-four, so y equals three quarters x plus six. To get the intercept form, move the constant to the right side to get three x minus four y equals minus twenty-four, and divide by minus twenty-four. The intercepts are minus eight and six.

slides.heading: Distance of a point from a line
slides.body_md: The distance of $(x_0, y_0)$ from $ax + by + c = 0$ is $d = \dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$, measured along the perpendicular.

visual.alt: The line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 meets the axes at A (4, 0) and B (0, 3). The point Q (4, 5) is joined to the line by a perpendicular that meets it at F (1.6, 1.8); the length QF is 4 units, which is |12 + 20 − 12| over 5.
visual.caption: The distance is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the line.

slides.narration: The distance from a point to a line is the length of the perpendicular. Substitute the point into the left side of the equation, take the absolute value, and divide by the square root of a squared plus b squared. In the figure the point four, five and the line three x plus four y minus twelve give twenty over five, which is four.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a distance
slides.body_md: Find the distance of $(6, 5)$ from $3x + 4y - 9 = 0$.

rows: Root of the sum of squares

visual.alt: Table: for the point 6, 5 and the line 3x plus 4y minus 9 equals 0, the expression equals 29, the root of 9 plus 16 is 5, so the distance is 29 over 5, which is 5.8 units.
visual.caption: $d = \dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

slides.narration: Put six and five into the expression three x plus four y minus nine. It gives twenty-nine. The root of nine plus sixteen is five. So the distance is twenty-nine over five, which is five point eight units. Always take the absolute value, because a distance cannot be negative.

slides.heading: Quick check: a distance
slides.body_md: The distance of the point minus five, seven from the line five x plus twelve y minus twenty equals zero is which value?
slides.narration: Substitute the point and divide by thirteen.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a distance in surd form
slides.body_md: Find the distance of $(3, 7)$ from $2x - 3y + 4 = 0$.

visual.alt: Table: for the point 3, 7 and the line 2x minus 3y plus 4 equals 0 the expression is minus 11, the root is root 13, so the distance is 11 over root 13, which is 11 root 13 over 13, about 3.05 units.
visual.caption: Take the modulus, then rationalise the denominator.

slides.narration: Substituting the point gives minus eleven. The root of four plus nine is root thirteen. The distance is eleven over root thirteen. To rationalise, multiply the top and bottom by root thirteen, giving eleven root thirteen over thirteen, which is about three point zero five units.

slides.heading: Distance between parallel lines
slides.body_md: For parallel lines $ax + by + c_1 = 0$ and $ax + by + c_2 = 0$ with the same $a$ and $b$: $d = \dfrac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

visual.alt: The parallel lines 4x + 3y − 12 = 0 and 4x + 3y + 8 = 0. The perpendicular from R (0, 4) on the first line meets the second line at S (−3.2, 1.6); the length RS is 4 units, which is |−12 − 8| over 5.
visual.caption: Parallel lines are a constant distance apart.

slides.narration: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart. First make the coefficients of x and y equal in both equations. Then the distance is the difference of the constants, in absolute value, divided by the square root of a squared plus b squared. In the figure the constants are minus twelve and eight, so the distance is twenty over five, which is four.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: unequal coefficients
slides.body_md: Find the distance between $6x - 8y + 15 = 0$ and $3x - 4y - 5 = 0$.

visual.alt: Table: the lines 6x minus 8y plus 15 equals 0 and 3x minus 4y minus 5 equals 0; writing the second as 6x minus 8y minus 10 equals 0, the distance is 25 over 10, which is 2.5 units.
visual.caption: $d = \dfrac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$ once $a$ and $b$ match.

slides.narration: The coefficients are different, so first double the second equation to get six x minus eight y minus ten equals zero. Now the constants are fifteen and minus ten, which differ by twenty-five. The root of thirty-six plus sixty-four is ten. So the distance is twenty-five over ten, or two point five units.

slides.heading: Quick check: not yet matched
slides.body_md: True or false: the parallel lines eight x plus six y minus fifteen and four x plus three y plus five are exactly two units apart.
slides.narration: Make the coefficients equal before using the formula.

slides.heading: Normal form (formative)
slides.body_md: The line at perpendicular distance $p > 0$ from the origin, whose perpendicular makes angle $\omega$ with the positive $x$-axis, is $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$. This slide is formative only.

visual.alt: The line 3x + 4y − 20 = 0. The perpendicular from the origin O meets it at F (2.4, 3.2), at distance p = 4. The perpendicular makes an angle of about 53.13 degrees with the positive x-axis, with cosine 3 over 5 and sine 4 over 5.
visual.caption: Normal form: $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$ with $p > 0$.

slides.narration: This idea is for practice and is not examined in the board paper. Draw the perpendicular from the origin to the line. Its length is p, and its direction makes an angle omega with the x axis. Then the equation is x cosine omega plus y sine omega equals p. In the figure, p is four, the cosine is three fifths and the sine is four fifths.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: reduce to normal form
slides.body_md: Reduce $x + y - 6 = 0$ to normal form.

visual.alt: Table: x plus y minus 6 equals 0 is x plus y equals 6; dividing by root 2 gives x over root 2 plus y over root 2 equals 3 root 2, so cosine and sine are both root 2 over 2, the angle is 45 degrees and p is 3 root 2.
visual.caption: Divide by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and keep $p$ positive.

slides.narration: Write the equation as x plus y equals six. The square root of one plus one is root two, so divide every term by root two. The cosine and the sine are both root two over two, which means the angle is forty-five degrees. The distance p is six over root two, which is three root two, a positive number as required.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Two-point form: slope from the points, then $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$
$d = \dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$; parallel lines: $\dfrac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$

visual.alt: Summary flow: the two-point and intercept forms write a line; the general form covers every line; the distance of a point from a line uses the modulus formula; the distance between parallel lines and the normal form follow from it.
visual.caption: Forms, distances and the normal form.

slides.narration: To sum up. The two-point form uses the slope between two points. The intercept form uses the two intercepts. notes.title: Straight Lines — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Slope and inclination
sections.body_md:
The **inclination** $\theta$ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis, $0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$. The **slope** is $m = \tan\theta$; a vertical line has none.

From two points, $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$. Positive slope: rising; negative: falling; zero: horizontal.

From $ax + by + c = 0$: $m = -\dfrac{a}{b}$ for $b \ne 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle $\theta$ a line makes with the positive $x$-axis.

visual.alt: Table of inclinations and slopes: 0 degrees gives slope 0; 30 degrees gives one over root three; 45 degrees gives 1; 60 degrees gives root three; a vertical line at 90 degrees has no slope; 120 degrees gives minus root three; 135 degrees gives minus 1.
visual.caption: The slope is the tangent of the inclination.

visuals.alt: The line through A (−3, −1) and B (5, 5) with a right-angled step under it: a horizontal run of 8 units from A, then a vertical rise of 6 units up to B. The slope is rise over run, six eighths, which is three quarters.
visuals.caption: Slope $=$ rise $\div$ run $= \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1: the line through P (−6, 1) and Q (3, −5) falls from left to right. Its slope is minus two thirds, so its inclination is an obtuse angle of about 146.31 degrees.
visuals.caption: A negative slope: the line falls, and the inclination is obtuse.

sections.heading: 2. Parallel, perpendicular and collinear
sections.body_md:
Non-vertical lines: parallel if $m_1 = m_2$; perpendicular if $m_1m_2 = -1$. A vertical and a horizontal line are perpendicular.

Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear if the slope of $AB$ equals the slope of $BC$.

For a line $ax + by + c = 0$, a parallel line keeps $a$ and $b$ and changes $c$; a perpendicular has the form $bx - ay + k = 0$.

visual.alt: Table of two pairs of lines: the first pair both have slope one half, so they are parallel; in the second pair the slopes are one half and minus two, whose product is minus one, so the lines are perpendicular.
visual.caption: Equal slopes: parallel. Product $-1$: perpendicular.

visuals.alt: Three lines: y = x/2 + 1 and y = x/2 − 2 are parallel, both with slope one half, and never meet; y = −2x + 6 has slope −2 and cuts the first line at M (2, 2) at right angles, because one half times minus two is minus one.
visuals.caption: Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$. Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

visuals.alt: Three points D (−5, 4), E (1, 1) and F (7, −2) on one straight line. The slope of DE and the slope of EF are both minus one half, and they share the point E.
visuals.caption: Equal slopes $DE$ and $EF$ with $E$ shared: collinear.

visuals.alt: Table: intercepts 5 and minus 3 give x over 5 plus y over minus 3 equals 1; multiplying by 15 gives 3x minus 5y minus 15 equals 0, and the point minus 5, minus 6 satisfies it.
visuals.caption: Intercepts are signed lengths along the axes.

sections.heading: 3. Angle between two lines
sections.body_md:
If $\theta$ is the acute angle between lines with slopes $m_1$, $m_2$: $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$. The obtuse angle is $180^\circ - \theta$.

If $1 + m_1m_2 = 0$ the lines are perpendicular. If one line is vertical, $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{1}{m}\right|$ for the other. For equations in general form the same angle has $\tan\theta = \dfrac{|a_1b_2 - a_2b_1|}{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2|}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The smaller of the two angles two intersecting lines make; the other is its supplement.

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of slopes with the tangent of the acute angle between the lines: 2 and one third give tangent 1, 45 degrees; 1 and one third give one half, 26.57 degrees; 3 and minus one half give 7, 81.87 degrees; 2 and minus one half make 1 plus m one m two equal to zero, so the lines are perpendicular at 90 degrees.
visual.caption: $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$; if $1 + m_1m_2 = 0$ the lines are perpendicular.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3: the lines x − 2y + 3 = 0 (slope one half) and 2x − y − 3 = 0 (slope 2) cross at P (3, 3). The tangent of the acute angle between them is three quarters, an angle of about 36.87 degrees.
visuals.caption: Slopes $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $2$: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$, $\theta \approx 36.87^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Table: the slopes are one half and 2; the tangent of the acute angle is three quarters; the angle is about 36.87 degrees; and the lines meet at the point 3, 3.
visuals.caption: Take the absolute value to get the acute angle.

sections.heading: 4. Point-slope and slope-intercept forms
sections.body_md:
Horizontal line: $y = k$. Vertical line: $x = h$.

Point-slope: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$. Slope-intercept: $y = mx + c$, where $c$ is the $y$-intercept.

A line parallel to a given one through a point keeps the slope; a perpendicular uses the negative reciprocal.

key_terms.definition_md: The value $c$ where the line meets the $y$-axis, at $(0, c)$.

rows: Parallel to the $x$-axis, $k$ above or below it
Parallel to the $y$-axis, $h$ to the right or left

visual.alt: Table of special lines: y equals k is horizontal with slope 0; x equals h is vertical with no slope; point-slope form is y minus y one equals m times x minus x one; and y equals m x plus c has slope m and y-intercept c.
visual.caption: Horizontal: slope $0$. Vertical: no slope.

visuals.alt: The line through T (2, −3) with slope two thirds, so that a step of 3 units across is a rise of 2 units; it also passes through U (5, −1). Its equation is 2x − 3y − 13 = 0.
visuals.caption: Point-slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.

visuals.alt: The line y = three quarters x − 2. It crosses the y-axis at C (0, −2), so the y-intercept is −2, and it passes through D (4, 1) and E (−4, −5): every 4 units across is a rise of 3 units.
visuals.caption: In $y = mx + c$: slope $m = \dfrac{3}{4}$, $y$-intercept $c = -2$.

rows: Parallel line has the same slope

visuals.alt: Table: the line through minus 1, minus 3 and 2, 5 has slope eight thirds; the parallel line through 4, 1 is y minus 1 equals eight thirds times x minus 4, which is 8x minus 3y minus 29 equals 0.
visuals.caption: A parallel line keeps the slope; only the point changes.

visuals.alt: Table: the line 2x plus 5y minus 4 equals 0 has slope minus two fifths, so a perpendicular has slope five halves; through 3, minus 1 it is y plus 1 equals five halves times x minus 3, which is 5x minus 2y minus 17 equals 0.
visuals.caption: Perpendicular slope: the negative reciprocal.

sections.heading: 5. Two-point and intercept forms
sections.body_md:
Two-point: $y - y_1 = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1)$.

Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$ for a line with $x$-intercept $a$ and $y$-intercept $b$, both nonzero. A line through the origin, or parallel to an axis, has no intercept form.

Always check a second point in the final equation.

key_terms.definition_md: The value $a$ where the line meets the $x$-axis, at $(a, 0)$.

visual.alt: The line through A (−3, −4) and B (6, 2). Its slope is six ninths, which is two thirds, and its equation is 2x − 3y − 6 = 0.
visual.caption: Two-point form: $y - y_1 = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1)$.

visuals.alt: Table: the line through minus 3, minus 4 and 6, 2 has slope two thirds; the two-point form gives 3y plus 12 equals 2x plus 6, so 2x minus 3y minus 6 equals 0, and the point 6, 2 satisfies it.
visuals.caption: Always check the second point in the final equation.

visuals.alt: The line with x-intercept 5 and y-intercept −3, through A (5, 0) and B (0, −3), and also through C (−5, −6). Its equation is x over 5 plus y over −3 equals 1, that is 3x − 5y − 15 = 0.
visuals.caption: Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$.

visuals.alt: Table: intercepts 5 and minus 3 give x over 5 plus y over minus 3 equals 1; multiplying by 15 gives 3x minus 5y minus 15 equals 0, and the point minus 5, minus 6 satisfies it.
visuals.caption: Intercepts are signed lengths along the axes.

sections.heading: 6. Distance of a point from a line
sections.body_md:
The perpendicular distance of $(x_0, y_0)$ from $ax + by + c = 0$ is $d = \dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$. The distance of the origin is $\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

Leave surd answers in rationalised form, for example $\dfrac{11\sqrt{13}}{13}$. The altitude of a triangle from a vertex is the distance of the vertex from the opposite side.

key_terms.definition_md: The shortest distance from a point to a line, measured along the perpendicular.

visual.alt: The line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 meets the axes at A (4, 0) and B (0, 3). The point Q (4, 5) is joined to the line by a perpendicular that meets it at F (1.6, 1.8); the length QF is 4 units, which is |12 + 20 − 12| over 5.
visual.caption: The distance is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the line.

rows: Root of the sum of squares

visuals.alt: Table: for the point 6, 5 and the line 3x plus 4y minus 9 equals 0, the expression equals 29, the root of 9 plus 16 is 5, so the distance is 29 over 5, which is 5.8 units.
visuals.caption: $d = \dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

visuals.alt: Table: for the point 3, 7 and the line 2x minus 3y plus 4 equals 0 the expression is minus 11, the root is root 13, so the distance is 11 over root 13, which is 11 root 13 over 13, about 3.05 units.
visuals.caption: Take the modulus, then rationalise the denominator.

sections.heading: 7. Distance between parallel lines
sections.body_md:
For $ax + by + c_1 = 0$ and $ax + by + c_2 = 0$: $d = \dfrac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$. The coefficients of $x$ and $y$ must be equal first.

A line half-way between two parallels has the mean of their constants.

key_terms.definition_md: Lines with equal slopes that never meet, a constant distance apart.

visual.alt: The parallel lines 4x + 3y − 12 = 0 and 4x + 3y + 8 = 0. The perpendicular from R (0, 4) on the first line meets the second line at S (−3.2, 1.6); the length RS is 4 units, which is |−12 − 8| over 5.
visual.caption: Parallel lines are a constant distance apart.

visuals.alt: Table: the lines 6x minus 8y plus 15 equals 0 and 3x minus 4y minus 5 equals 0; writing the second as 6x minus 8y minus 10 equals 0, the distance is 25 over 10, which is 2.5 units.
visuals.caption: $d = \dfrac{|c_1 - c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$ once $a$ and $b$ match.

sections.heading: 8. General equation and normal form (formative only)
sections.body_md:
This section is for practice and is not examined in the board paper.

General equation $Ax + By + C = 0$: slope $-\dfrac{A}{B}$, intercepts $-\dfrac{C}{A}$ and $-\dfrac{C}{B}$.

Normal form $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$ with $p > 0$: divide by $\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$ and change signs so that $p$ is positive.

key_terms.definition_md: $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$, where $p > 0$ is the distance of the line from the origin.

visual.alt: Table of the general equation A x plus B y plus C equals 0: the slope is minus A over B, the x-intercept is minus C over A and the y-intercept is minus C over B; if B is 0 the line is vertical, if A is 0 it is horizontal, and if C is 0 it passes through the origin.
visual.caption: One equation $Ax + By + C = 0$ covers every straight line.

visuals.alt: Table for 3x minus 4y plus 24 equals 0: the slope-intercept form is y equals three quarters x plus 6; the intercept form is x over minus 8 plus y over 6 equals 1; the intercepts are minus 8 and 6.
visuals.caption: Solve for $y$ for the slope; divide by $-C$ for the intercepts.

visuals.alt: The line 3x + 4y − 20 = 0. The perpendicular from the origin O meets it at F (2.4, 3.2), at distance p = 4. The perpendicular makes an angle of about 53.13 degrees with the positive x-axis, with cosine 3 over 5 and sine 4 over 5.
visuals.caption: Normal form: $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$ with $p > 0$.

visuals.alt: Table: x plus y minus 6 equals 0 is x plus y equals 6; dividing by root 2 gives x over root 2 plus y over root 2 equals 3 root 2, so cosine and sine are both root 2 over 2, the angle is 45 degrees and p is 3 root 2.
visuals.caption: Divide by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and keep $p$ positive.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Slope, parallel or perpendicular test (1–2 marks):* the formula, the substitution and the value.
- *Angle between lines (2–3 marks):* both slopes, the tangent formula, the angle; mention the obtuse angle if asked.
- *Equation of a line (2–3 marks):* name the form, substitute, simplify to $ax + by + c = 0$, and check a point.
- *Distance (2–3 marks):* substitute into the modulus formula, evaluate the root, state the units.
- *Parallel lines and triangles (3–5 marks):* match the coefficients, or find the altitude as a distance, then the area.

**Common mistakes**
1. Dividing run by rise.
2. Dropping the modulus in the angle or distance formula.
3. Using the negative of the slope instead of the negative reciprocal.
4. Using the parallel-distance formula with unequal coefficients.
5. Swapping the $x$- and $y$-intercepts in the intercept form.
6. Forgetting that a vertical line has no slope.
7. Leaving a surd distance with an irrational denominator.

cards.front_md: What is the inclination of a line?
cards.back_md: The angle $\theta$ the line makes with the positive $x$-axis, $0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Slope in terms of the inclination?
cards.back_md: $m = \tan\theta$. A vertical line has no slope.

cards.front_md: Slope from two points?
cards.back_md: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$.

cards.front_md: What does the sign of the slope tell you?
cards.back_md: Positive: rising. Negative: falling. Zero: horizontal.

cards.front_md: Slope of $ax + by + c = 0$?
cards.back_md: $-\dfrac{a}{b}$ (for $b \ne 0$).

cards.front_md: Condition for parallel lines?
cards.back_md: $m_1 = m_2$ (and the lines are distinct).

cards.front_md: Condition for perpendicular lines?
cards.back_md: $m_1m_2 = -1$, or one line vertical and the other horizontal.

cards.front_md: How do you test three points for collinearity?
cards.back_md: The slopes of two segments sharing a point must be equal.

cards.front_md: Formula for the acute angle between two lines?
cards.back_md: $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}\right|$.

cards.front_md: What if $1 + m_1m_2 = 0$?
cards.back_md: The lines are perpendicular; the angle is $90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: The obtuse angle between two lines?
cards.back_md: $180^\circ - \theta$, where $\theta$ is the acute angle.

cards.front_md: Equation of a horizontal line? A vertical line?
cards.back_md: $y = k$ and $x = h$.

cards.front_md: Point-slope form?
Slope-intercept form?
cards.back_md: $y = mx + c$, with $y$-intercept $c$.

cards.front_md: Two-point form?
Intercept form?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$, with intercepts $a$ and $b$.

cards.front_md: Which lines have no intercept form?
cards.back_md: Lines through the origin and lines parallel to an axis.

cards.front_md: Parallel line to $ax + by + c = 0$ through a point?
cards.back_md: Keep $a$ and $b$; find the new $c$ from the point.

cards.front_md: Perpendicular line to $ax + by + c = 0$?
cards.back_md: It has the form $bx - ay + k = 0$.

cards.front_md: How do you find the intercepts of $ax + by + c = 0$?
cards.back_md: Put $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept $-\dfrac{c}{a}$; put $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept $-\dfrac{c}{b}$.

cards.front_md: Distance of $(x_0, y_0)$ from $ax + by + c = 0$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

cards.front_md: Distance of the origin from $ax + by + c = 0$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

cards.front_md: Distance between $ax + by + c_1 = 0$ and $ax + by + c_2 = 0$?
What must you do before using the parallel-distance formula?
cards.back_md: Make the coefficients of $x$ and $y$ equal in both equations.

cards.front_md: How do you find the altitude of a triangle by coordinates?
cards.back_md: It is the distance of the vertex from the line through the opposite side.

cards.front_md: What is the line half-way between two parallels?
cards.back_md: The same $a$, $b$ with $c$ equal to the mean of the two constants.

cards.front_md: Why is the distance formula along the perpendicular?
cards.back_md: The perpendicular is the shortest segment from the point to the line.

cards.front_md: Formative only: the general equation of a line?
cards.back_md: $Ax + By + C = 0$: slope $-\dfrac{A}{B}$, intercepts $-\dfrac{C}{A}$ and $-\dfrac{C}{B}$.

cards.front_md: Formative only: the normal form?
cards.back_md: $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$ with $p > 0$, the distance of the line from the origin.

cards.front_md: Formative only: how do you reduce $ax + by + c = 0$ to normal form?
cards.back_md: Divide by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, after changing signs so the constant on the right is positive.

questions.stem_md: The segment joining $A(-5, 4)$ and $B(3, -8)$ lies on a line whose slope is
questions.solution_md: $m = \dfrac{-8 - 4}{3 - (-5)} = \dfrac{-12}{8} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$. Reversing the sign gives $\dfrac{3}{2}$, and the run-over-rise values are $-\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: A straight line is inclined at $120^\circ$ to the positive direction of the $x$-axis. Its slope is
questions.solution_md: $m = \tan 120^\circ = -\tan 60^\circ = -\sqrt{3}$. The value $\sqrt{3}$ loses the sign, while $\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ belong to $30^\circ$ and $150^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The straight line $9x + 4y - 11 = 0$ has slope
questions.solution_md: Solving for $y$: $4y = -9x + 11$, so $y = -\dfrac{9}{4}x + \dfrac{11}{4}$ and the slope is $-\dfrac{9}{4}$. The value $\dfrac{9}{4}$ drops the sign, $-\dfrac{4}{9}$ is inverted, and $\dfrac{11}{4}$ is the $y$-intercept.

questions.stem_md: The lines $kx + 6y - 5 = 0$ and $8x + 3y + 2 = 0$ are parallel for $k$ equal to
questions.solution_md: Parallel lines have equal slopes: $-\dfrac{k}{6} = -\dfrac{8}{3}$, so $k = 16$. The value $-\dfrac{9}{4}$ comes from the perpendicular condition $8k + 18 = 0$, $4$ from cross-multiplying the wrong way ($6k = 24$), and $48$ from multiplying $6 \times 8$.

questions.stem_md: The lines $6x + ky - 1 = 0$ and $10x - 12y + 7 = 0$ meet at right angles when $k$ is
questions.solution_md: The slopes are $-\dfrac{6}{k}$ and $\dfrac{10}{12} = \dfrac{5}{6}$, and their product must be $-1$: $-\dfrac{6}{k} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = -1$ gives $k = 5$. The values $\mp\dfrac{36}{5}$ come from the parallel condition.

questions.stem_md: The acute angle between the lines $3x - y + 4 = 0$ and $2x + y - 9 = 0$ is
questions.solution_md: The slopes are $m_1 = 3$ and $m_2 = -2$, so $\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{3 - (-2)}{1 + 3(-2)}\right| = \left|\dfrac{5}{-5}\right| = 1$ and $\theta = 45^\circ$. The angle $135^\circ$ is the obtuse angle between the same two lines.

questions.stem_md: The points $P(-3, 8)$, $Q(1, 2)$ and $R(k, -4)$ lie on one straight line. Then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: Slope of $PQ = \dfrac{2 - 8}{1 + 3} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$, and slope of $QR = \dfrac{-4 - 2}{k - 1}$. Equating: $\dfrac{-6}{k - 1} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$ gives $k - 1 = 4$, so $k = 5$. A sign slip gives $-3$, and inverting the slope gives $k - 1 = 9$, so $k = 10$.

questions.stem_md: The line through $(2, -1)$ and $(k, 5)$ is parallel to the line $3x - 2y + 7 = 0$. The value of $k$ is
questions.solution_md: The given line has slope $\dfrac{3}{2}$, so $\dfrac{5 - (-1)}{k - 2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, i.e. $k - 2 = 4$ and $k = 6$. The value $-7$ comes from using the perpendicular slope $-\dfrac{2}{3}$, $11$ from inverting the slope, and $4$ from taking the slope as $3$.

questions.stem_md: The line that passes through $(6, -1)$ with slope $-\dfrac{2}{3}$ has the equation
questions.solution_md: Point-slope form: $y + 1 = -\dfrac{2}{3}(x - 6)$, so $3y + 3 = -2x + 12$ and $2x + 3y - 9 = 0$. Using slope $\dfrac{2}{3}$ gives $2x - 3y - 15 = 0$, the point $(-6, 1)$ gives $2x + 3y + 9 = 0$, and slope $-\dfrac{3}{2}$ gives $3x + 2y - 16 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: The straight line through $A(-4, 7)$ and $B(8, -2)$ has the equation
questions.solution_md: Slope $= \dfrac{-2 - 7}{8 + 4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}$, so $y - 7 = -\dfrac{3}{4}(x + 4)$ and $3x + 4y - 16 = 0$. The line $3x - 4y + 40 = 0$ has the wrong sign of slope, $4x + 3y - 5 = 0$ inverts it, and $3x + 4y + 16 = 0$ has the wrong constant: it misses both points.

questions.stem_md: A straight line makes an intercept of $-4$ on the $x$-axis and $6$ on the $y$-axis. Its equation is
questions.solution_md: Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{-4} + \dfrac{y}{6} = 1$. Multiplying by $12$: $-3x + 2y = 12$, that is $3x - 2y + 12 = 0$. Swapping the intercepts gives $2x - 3y - 12 = 0$, and changing a sign gives $3x + 2y - 12 = 0$ or $3x - 2y - 12 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: The line $5x - 12y + 60 = 0$ cuts the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis at distances (with sign) equal to
questions.solution_md: Put $y = 0$: $5x = -60$, so the $x$-intercept is $-12$. Put $x = 0$: $-12y = -60$, so the $y$-intercept is $5$. The other options swap the intercepts or change signs. Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{-12} + \dfrac{y}{5} = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The line drawn through $(-7, 2)$ at right angles to the $x$-axis has the equation
questions.solution_md: A line perpendicular to the $x$-axis is vertical, so every point on it has the same $x$-coordinate, $-7$: the line is $x = -7$. The line $y = 2$ is the horizontal line through the same point.

questions.stem_md: The line through $(-1, 4)$ that is perpendicular to the line $3x - 5y + 8 = 0$ has the equation
questions.solution_md: The given line has slope $\dfrac{3}{5}$, so the perpendicular has slope $-\dfrac{5}{3}$. Then $y - 4 = -\dfrac{5}{3}(x + 1)$ gives $5x + 3y - 7 = 0$. The line $3x - 5y + 23 = 0$ is parallel to the given one, $3x + 5y - 17 = 0$ negates only the sign, and $5x - 3y + 17 = 0$ inverts only the fraction.

questions.stem_md: How far, measured perpendicularly, is the point $(-5, 7)$ from the line $5x + 12y - 20 = 0$?
questions.solution_md: $d = \dfrac{|5(-5) + 12(7) - 20|}{\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2}} = \dfrac{|39|}{13} = 3$. The value $39$ forgets the denominator, $\dfrac{3}{13}$ divides by $13^2$ instead of $13$, and $\dfrac{39}{17}$ uses $5 + 12$ under the root sign.

questions.stem_md: Two parallel roads on a grid are drawn as $3x + 4y + 8 = 0$ and $6x + 8y - 14 = 0$. The gap between them is
questions.solution_md: First make the coefficients equal: $6x + 8y - 14 = 0$ is $3x + 4y - 7 = 0$. Then $d = \dfrac{|8 - (-7)|}{\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}} = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$. Using $-14$ directly gives $\dfrac{22}{5}$, dividing $22$ by $10$ gives $\dfrac{11}{5}$, and $|8 - 7|$ gives $\dfrac{1}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: The point $(k, 2)$ with $k > 0$ is at distance $3$ from the line $4x - 3y + 7 = 0$. Then $k$ equals

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Slope of $PQ = \dfrac{1 - 5}{6 + 2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. Then $y - 5 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x + 2)$ gives $x + 2y - 8 = 0$.

**(b)** The altitude is perpendicular to $PQ$, so its slope is $2$. Through $R(2, -5)$: $y + 5 = 2(x - 2)$ gives $2x - y - 9 = 0$.

**(c)** Solve $x + 2y = 8$ and $2x - y = 9$: from the second, $y = 2x - 9$, so $x + 4x - 18 = 8$ and $x = \dfrac{26}{5}$, $y = \dfrac{7}{5}$. So $F\left(\dfrac{26}{5}, \dfrac{7}{5}\right)$.

**(d)** $RF = \dfrac{|2 + 2(-5) - 8|}{\sqrt{1^2 + 2^2}} = \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{16\sqrt{5}}{5}$ units. (Check: $RF^2 = \left(\dfrac{16}{5}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{32}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1280}{25} = \dfrac{256}{5}$.)

**(e)** $PQ = \sqrt{8^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}$, so the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4\sqrt{5} \times \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{5}} = 32$ square units.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$ the vertices are $A(-2, 1)$, $B(10, 6)$ and $C(1, -1)$. Find (a) the length $AB$; (b) the equation of $AB$; (c) the length of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$; (d) the area of the triangle; (e) the equation of the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$, and its distance from $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $AB = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ units.

**(b)** Slope $= \dfrac{6 - 1}{10 + 2} = \dfrac{5}{12}$, so $y - 1 = \dfrac{5}{12}(x + 2)$ gives $5x - 12y + 22 = 0$.

**(c)** The altitude is the distance of $C$ from $AB$: $\dfrac{|5(1) - 12(-1) + 22|}{\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2}} = \dfrac{39}{13} = 3$ units.

**(d)** Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 13 \times 3 = \dfrac{39}{2} = 19.5$ square units.

**(e)** The parallel through $C$ has the same slope: $y + 1 = \dfrac{5}{12}(x - 1)$, so $5x - 12y - 17 = 0$. The distance between the two parallel lines is $\dfrac{|22 - (-17)|}{13} = 3$ units, the same as the altitude.

questions.solution_md: Length, line, then the point-line distance as the altitude; parallel lines are as far apart as the altitude.

questions.stem_md: (Formative practice.) (a) Reduce $12x - 5y + 52 = 0$ to the normal form $x\cos\omega + y\sin\omega = p$ and state $p$, $\cos\omega$ and $\sin\omega$. (b) Find the equation of the line for which $p = 6$, $\cos\omega = \dfrac{8}{17}$ and $\sin\omega = \dfrac{15}{17}$. (c) Show that the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the line in (a) is $\left(-\dfrac{48}{13}, \dfrac{20}{13}\right)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13$. The constant $52$ is positive, so write $-12x + 5y = 52$ and divide by $13$: $-\dfrac{12}{13}x + \dfrac{5}{13}y = 4$. So $p = 4$, $\cos\omega = -\dfrac{12}{13}$ and $\sin\omega = \dfrac{5}{13}$.

**(b)** $\dfrac{8}{17}x + \dfrac{15}{17}y = 6$, and multiplying by $17$: $8x + 15y = 102$, that is $8x + 15y - 102 = 0$.

**(c)** The foot is $(p\cos\omega, p\sin\omega) = \left(4 \times \left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right), 4 \times \dfrac{5}{13}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{48}{13}, \dfrac{20}{13}\right)$. Check: $12\left(-\dfrac{48}{13}\right) - 5\left(\dfrac{20}{13}\right) + 52 = \dfrac{-576 - 100 + 676}{13} = 0$.

questions.solution_md: p is the distance from the origin; the foot of the perpendicular is p cos omega, p sin omega.
